name: Ouroboros Energy Kinetic Bleed Capacitor
description:
The Kinetic Bleed Capacitor is a wearable energy harvesting and storage unit that converts ambient kinetic and thermal energy from its user's movement, environmental vibration, and body heat into usable electrical charge. It mounts as a rigid dorsal pack roughly the size of a hardback book, connected via a mesh of piezoelectric filaments woven into a load-bearing vest. Under normal activity — walking, climbing, operating machinery — it accumulates a slow trickle charge stored in a dense graphene supercapacitor array. Under high-exertion scenarios such as combat or sprinting, charge accumulation accelerates dramatically.

What distinguishes the KBC from competing portable power cells is its dual-mode discharge architecture. It can bleed stored energy slowly into connected devices — maintaining a hacking rig, powering a medical automaton, sustaining a signal relay — or it can dump its entire charge in a single directed burst through a contact interface, functioning as an improvised high-voltage discharge weapon or a breaching tool capable of frying electronic locks and sensor grids. This dual use makes it uniquely dangerous in the eyes of regulators, who classify it differently depending on jurisdiction.

The KBC is ubiquitous among couriers, scavengers, and off-grid operators who cannot rely on municipal charging infrastructure. In the deeper residential stacks of GLMZ, where power rationing is enforced by OUROBOROS ENERGY's own metering systems, the KBC is both a survival tool and a political statement — a way of reclaiming energy from the grid that extracts it from you. Corporate security teams have learned to scan for them at checkpoints, not because of the burst-discharge capability, but because operatives use them to power equipment that should be dead.
tactical_use: Operatives use the KBC to maintain power-hungry equipment — hacking rigs, drones, medical units — without relying on disposable cells that leave a procurement trail. The burst-discharge function is used to fry electronic door locks, disable proximity sensors, and in close-quarters situations, incapacitate unarmored targets through conductive contact. Couriers running dead zones use it to guarantee their comms and navigation stay live. It is also used to jump-start vehicles, power breaching charges, and keep cybernetic systems running when a user's internal power supply is compromised.
cultural_context: In the lower stacks, carrying a KBC is a marker of self-sufficiency and distrust of the grid. OUROBOROS ENERGY's tiered metering system means that residents who draw above their allotment face punitive rates or outright cutoffs — the KBC is a workaround that has become a cultural symbol of resistance. Graffiti in stack districts sometimes depicts a KBC with the OUROBOROS logo crossed out. In corporate circles, the device is viewed as low-status survival gear, but off-grid teams and black-site operators value it precisely because it generates no purchase signature from a charging point.
story_hooks: A KBC recovered from a dead courier contains a residual charge pattern that — when analyzed — encodes a message, suggesting the courier was using charge-bleed timing as a dead-drop signal method.

OUROBOROS ENERGY has quietly pushed legislation in two districts to reclassify the burst-discharge function as a prohibited weapon, effectively banning the device — the players are asked to transport a shipment before the ban takes effect.

A modified KBC is found at a crime scene with the burst-discharge circuit bypassed to deliver a continuous high-voltage output — it was used as an execution tool, and the modification requires specialized knowledge that points to a specific manufacturer's workshop.

The players' KBC malfunctions during a run in a Faraday-shielded facility, dumping its entire charge into a connected medical automaton and triggering an emergency in the middle of a stealth operation.

physical_description.visual_profile: A rigid geometric dorsal pack with a distinctive segmented spine. The main unit resembles a hardback book stood upright, but with a pronounced central ribbed column running vertically down its back. The graphene supercapacitor array within is visible through translucent side panels, revealing a honeycomb lattice of copper-colored cells arranged in cascading tiers. The entire assembly has an organic-mechanical quality—something between exoskeleton and distributed nervous system.
physical_description.dimensions: 28cm tall x 18cm wide x 9cm deep dorsal unit; vest integration adds approximately 5cm to torso width
physical_description.weight_description: 2.1kg fully charged—substantial enough to feel when moving, requiring the load-bearing vest to distribute weight evenly across shoulders and lower back
physical_description.primary_material: Anodized aluminum chassis with transparent polycarbonate side panels; graphene supercapacitor substrate; piezoelectric filament mesh woven into vest fabric (ultra-high modulus synthetic polymer blend)
physical_description.finish: Satin-brushed aluminum with visible mechanical fasteners; polycarbonate panels have a subtle iridescent anti-reflective coating; copper traces visible beneath transparent sections show active charge pathways
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray dorsal unit with burnt-orange accent striping along the ribbed spine; copper-tone capacitor cells glowing warm amber internally; the load-bearing vest is charcoal with reflective thread mesh forming a circuit-board pattern across the chest and shoulders
physical_description.interface_elements: Rear-facing three-position toggle switch (5V/12V/24V continuous output); a single recessed pushbutton for burst-discharge mode (ringed with a red LED that pulses when charge exceeds 80%); four color-coded modular connector ports (USB-C, barrel jack, wireless induction pad, high-voltage contact interface); a small dot-matrix LCD screen displaying charge percentage, active voltage, and thermal status; charge-rate indicator bar formed by tiny LEDs running down one edge of the ribbed spine
distinctive_features: Translucent polycarbonate side panels revealing the honeycomb graphene capacitor lattice, which glows faintly under load
Vertical ribbed spine that acts as both structural support and primary thermal dissipation channel
Piezoelectric filament mesh visible as fine copper threading throughout the load-bearing vest—creates a subtle shimmer when light catches it
Single dominant red burst-discharge indicator LED that pulses with charging state
The connector interface module protrudes slightly from the lower rear, angled for quick hot-swap access
Mechanical design uses exposed fasteners and modular sections, giving it a 'kit-built' aesthetic common to tier 3-4 equipment
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: OUROBOROS ENERGY logo stamped in metallic gray on the upper dorsal unit; regulatory stamps in micro-print along the bottom edge (includes GLMZ energy declaration and tier-availability notation); serial number etched on rear connector module; small warning symbol (lightning bolt + spark) repeated on both polycarbonate panels
physical_description.condition_typical: In active use, the device shows faint heat shimmer along the ribbed spine during high-exertion scenarios. The internal graphene lattice appears to shift color subtly—deepening from amber to orange—as charge accumulates. Minor scuffing and micro-scratches on the aluminum chassis are normal. Piezoelectric mesh on the vest shows wear patterns consistent with body movement (compression creases at shoulders and lower back). The red burst-discharge LED pulses steadily during standby, faster during active charging.

The unit's red burst-discharge LED pulses, creating a rhythmic glow. Mounted on a stark white or brushed-metal workbench surrounded by modular connectors, a handheld power tester, and OUROBOROS ENERGY product documentation.
